paras: The Mandan citizens' order to Ira Hall and John Trumbull to leave town was a threat of lynching made on August 28, 1882, when a mass meeting in Mandan, Dakota Territory, sent a committee to tell the two men, accused in the killing of Jacob Book, to leave by noon the next day. Hall promised to go and Trumbull disappeared, and no report shows that either man was harmed. Territorial papers treated the meeting as the climax of local anger at a federal commissioner who had freed one of the accused.

In mid-August 1882 Jacob Book was clubbed near Fort Lincoln and died at the fort, and soldiers and Sheriff Carr arrested Charles Trumbull, Ira Hall and John Trumbull, a young Mandan lawyer. A coroner's jury at Mandan returned a verdict of murder against all three on August 17, and both the Jamestown Alert and the Yankton Dakotaian reported threats to lynch them, against which the sheriff prepared.

Because the killing took place on a reservation, the case went before a United States commissioner at Bismarck. By August 22 the commissioner, whom the dispatch called Judge Corey, had held Charles Trumbull and Hall for manslaughter, released them on bail and dismissed John Trumbull, causing what a Bismarck dispatch called "general surprise and disappointment."

Hall crossed from Bismarck into Mandan on Saturday, August 26, and John Trumbull appeared on the town's streets on Monday, August 28. A mass meeting was called at once, and according to the Dakotaian's Mandan dispatch it appointed a committee of eight "of the best citizens" to give the two men until noon the next day to leave town. The committee found Hall at his residence and he promised to leave, but Trumbull had disappeared and the committee began searching for him.

The committee reported back to the crowd at the court house, which the Dakotaian put at 250 and the Alert at about 300. The Dakotaian wrote that the town was full of "railroad men and others" determined to be rid of the men, and that Trumbull, if found, would be told to leave "or stand the consequences." The Alert's informant, a Mandan resident, was blunter, saying the two men would be lynched if found in Mandan after Tuesday noon.

No report of what happened at the deadline, or of Trumbull being found, appears in the coverage. In November, at Fargo, indictments were brought for the murder of Book against Hall and both Trumbulls, and Charles Trumbull was tried in the United States court and acquitted. The Bismarck Tribune remarked that "Mandan is all broke up because Trumbull was acquitted," and quoted the Fargo Argus on a rumor, "not generally believed," that the three men would be lynched if they returned to Mandan.

The episode appeared in two Dakota papers: a Mandan dispatch in the Yankton Press and Daily Dakotaian of August 31 and a combined informant's report and Mandan special in the Jamestown Weekly Alert of September 1, reprinted from its Tuesday daily. Both papers presented the citizens' anger as a response to the commissioner's "remarkable" decision and described the committee in approving terms, without criticizing the threat. The Alert, which noted that Book was a former Jamestown resident, headlined its item "Excitement at Mandan" and passed on the lynching threat without comment.
None of the reports gives the race of the accused men or of Book.

accounts.label: Mandan dispatch (Dakotaian)
accounts.gist: A committee of eight gave Hall and Trumbull until noon the next day to leave; Trumbull, if found, would be told to leave 'or stand the consequences' before a crowd of 250.

accounts.label: Mandan informant and special (Alert)
accounts.gist: A prominent Mandan resident and a Mandan special said the two men would be lynched if found in town after Tuesday noon; about 300 attended the meeting.

framing.detail: The Dakotaian headed the dispatch 'Unpopular' [OCR 'Uapopnlar'] and described the committee as 'the best citizens', calling the commissioner's decision 'remarkable'.
The Jamestown Alert, headlined 'Excitement at Mandan', relayed that the men 'will be lynched' without comment and called the killing of a former Jamestown resident 'cruel'.

conflicts.note: Both Mandan reports of the same meeting; neither is clearly better.
